question: Will bidding in the FCC upper C-band auction conclude by 31 December 2027?
rationale: Bidding starts on 27 April 2027 under final rules, and the law requires the auction by July 2027. Similar auctions with clock and assignment phases took about 10-13 weeks (Auctions 107 and 110), so a normal auction closes in July 2027. That leaves about five months of slack. The main risks are litigation, an aviation or satellite dispute that delays the start, a government shutdown, or a long bidding war.
resolution: Yes if the FCC announces the close of bidding (clock and assignment phases) of Auction 115 by 31 Dec 2027.
signposts: Short-form filings close on schedule (6-20 January 2027); the qualified-bidder list appears (around March 2027); bidding actually opens on 27 April 2027.

question: Will the upper C-band auction clear above $0.94 per MHz-pop on today's 335M population, the 2021 lower C-band's headline price (about 8% above its $0.87 like-for-like)?
rationale: On the question's 335M-pop basis the 2021 lower C-band was about $0.87, so beating $0.94 means gross bids above $50.4B. Our price forecast puts about a 32% chance on that if the auction finishes, times about 95% that it finishes by end-2028. Getting there essentially needs SpaceX to bid hard against Verizon, or a fight for blocks next to existing C-band holdings. Heavy add-on costs and carrier balance sheets make it less likely than not.
resolution: Yes if Auction 115 gross bids divided by (MHz offered x 335M pops) exceed $0.94 and bidding concludes by 31 Dec 2028; No otherwise.
signposts: SpaceX on the qualified-bidder list (early 2027); total upfront payments and bidding eligibility (high eligibility signals demand); gross bids passing $50B in the clock phase.

question: Will SpaceX win licences in the upper C-band auction?
rationale: SpaceX took part in the Auction 115 rulemaking, won small licences in the 2026 AWS-3 re-auction, and has the cash and the stated aim to become a full mobile operator. With 3,248 licences on offer, it could win cheap rural blocks if it enters. Against that, the FCC refused to let satellite coverage count toward buildout, so licences carry ground-network obligations, and Musk called 800 MHz the last critical piece. We put about two-thirds on SpaceX applying and about two-thirds on it winning something if it does.
resolution: Yes if SpaceX or an affiliate is a winning bidder in Auction 115 by 31 Dec 2028.
signposts: The public list of short-form applicants (late January 2027); the qualified-bidder list (around March 2027); SpaceX comments on terrestrial plans at its Q4 2026 results.

question: Will SpaceX's purchase of EchoStar's AWS-4 and H-block licences close by the end of 2027?
rationale: The FCC approved the transfer in May 2026, the licences have sat in a trust since 22 May 2026, and closing is targeted for 30 November 2027. SpaceX is funding EchoStar's interest through November 2027, which supports that date. The risk is timing: there is only one month of slack before the deadline, and the Dish DBS and Dish Wireless bankruptcy cases add litigation risk. Both sides have strong reasons to close on time.
resolution: Yes if the licence assignment is consummated (not just approved) by 31 Dec 2027.
signposts: Any change to the 30 November 2027 target in EchoStar or SpaceX filings; rulings in the Dish DBS and Dish Wireless Chapter 11 cases; SpaceX confirming the $8.5B cash payment ahead of closing.

question: Will the FCC approve SpaceX's purchase of Grain's 800 MHz licences by the end of 2027?
rationale: The FCC accepted the filing on 10 November 2026, with petitions due 1 December and oppositions 8 December. Its informal 180-day review points to a decision around mid-2027, leaving about six months of buffer. This FCC approved every major 2025-26 transfer, including SpaceX-EchoStar in about eight months, and SpaceX holds no other low-band, so the concentration screen does not bind. The remaining risks are public-safety interference objections at 800 MHz, conditions that slow the order, or political friction.
resolution: Yes if the FCC grants the assignment applications (with or without conditions) by 31 Dec 2027.
signposts: Who files petitions to deny by 1 December 2026 (AT&T, Verizon or public-safety groups); any pause in the FCC's 180-day clock; an order by mid-2027.

question: Will SpaceX sell US mobile phone service under its own brand on its own spectrum by the end of 2028?
rationale: SpaceX has told investors it plans a US consumer mobile service on its own spectrum, targeting early 2028, once the EchoStar deal closes around 30 November 2027. Many phones already support Dish's band 70 frequencies, which helps. But that leaves only about 13 months, and SpaceX timelines, next-generation satellite launches and Starship cadence usually slip 6-12 months. A satellite-only or bundled plan billed by SpaceX would also count, which keeps this near a coin flip.
resolution: Yes if SpaceX/Starlink offers a paid US consumer mobile plan billed by SpaceX that uses SpaceX-owned spectrum (satellite, terrestrial or both) by 31 Dec 2028.
signposts: The EchoStar closing on schedule (30 November 2027); the first next-generation direct-to-cell satellite launches (2027); a SpaceX plan announcement, beta or pricing in the first half of 2028.

question: Will SpaceX be one of the four largest US mobile operators by subscribers by 2035?
rationale: SpaceX would need to pass the smaller of Charter and Comcast, which we expect at roughly 20-30M lines by 2035. That means 20M or more directly billed subscribers from a launch around 2028. Cable took about 8 years to reach 24M lines with bundles and free lines, Dish never scaled on its own, and satellites cannot carry dense indoor demand. The probability rests mainly on buying a subscriber base or a very cheap plan that scales fast.
resolution: Yes if SpaceX's directly billed US mobile subscribers exceed those of the fourth-largest of AT&T, Verizon, T-Mobile, Charter and Comcast at end-2035.
signposts: SpaceX direct US subscribers at end-2029 (above 3M would raise this sharply); any SpaceX purchase of a carrier or reseller base; large tower or site deals that give it urban coverage.

question: Will SpaceX, Amazon or another non-telecom tech company agree to buy a US facilities-based mobile carrier or a cable company's mobile business by 2030?
rationale: No non-telecom tech company has bought a US facilities-based carrier in 30 years; Google Fi and others stayed resellers. SpaceX needs towers, operations and customers, and even a small regional carrier would count, which lifts the odds above that base rate. Amazon's Globalstar deal shows appetite for spectrum assets. But Musk's stated approach is to build, not buy, the big three are effectively unbuyable, and cable mobile is core to the broadband bundle.
resolution: Yes if such a definitive agreement is announced by 31 Dec 2030.
signposts: Whether SpaceX signs tower leases or instead holds M&A talks (2027-28); Amazon's plans after Globalstar closes and its satellite-to-phone launch (around 2028); strategic reviews at regional carriers.

question: Will US wireless revenue per GB rise year on year in any year from 2027 to 2030, a sign of a capacity crunch?
rationale: For revenue per GB to rise, traffic growth would have to fall below revenue growth of about 2-4% in some year. CTIA traffic growth has not been below 14% since at least 2010, and our central path stays at 12-18% through 2030. Even our slow case keeps growth near 8-10%. The remaining chance is mostly a CTIA method change, such as splitting out fixed wireless, or carriers sharply throttling fixed wireless.
resolution: Yes if CTIA-basis service revenue per GB of traffic is higher than the prior year for any of 2027, 2028, 2029 or 2030.
signposts: CTIA traffic growth in each September survey from 2027; BLS wireless price index after carrier price rises; any carrier pausing fixed wireless sales.

question: Will US mobile data traffic grow more than 25% in any year from 2027 to 2030?
rationale: US traffic growth fell from 38% in 2022 to 20% in 2025, and our central path keeps it at 12-18% for 2027-30. A year above 25% needs a new driver: cheap fixed wireless on new upper C-band capacity, an AI uplink surge, or a CTIA method change. The series has jumped 12 points or more three times since 2018, and four annual chances keep this from being negligible. The research team's own estimate was 15%.
resolution: Yes if CTIA-reported annual traffic growth exceeds 25% for any of 2027-2030.
signposts: CTIA's 2026 growth figure (around September 2027); Ericsson's North American growth readings; fixed wireless adds re-accelerating once upper C-band is deployed (2028-30).

question: Will a US carrier launch commercial 3GPP 6G service by the end of 2030?
rationale: 3GPP's Release 21 final spec freeze is March 2029. The first US 5G launch came about 10-13 months after its freeze and LTE about 21 months, so a first 6G launch lands between late 2029 and late 2030, right at the deadline. T-Mobile says it will be first around 2030, Ericsson expects first commercial systems in 2030, and a small paid launch for marketing would count. Against that are flat capex, weak returns, no new 7 GHz spectrum by 2030, and any 3GPP slip.
resolution: Yes if any US carrier offers paid commercial service on 3GPP Release 21 (6G) radio by 31 Dec 2030.
signposts: The Release 21 stage-3 freeze holding at December 2028; 6G chipset and handset announcements for 2029-30; carrier 6G trial and launch announcements.

question: Will the FCC finish auctioning any upper mid-band spectrum above 4.2 GHz (such as 7.125-7.4 GHz) by the end of 2030?
rationale: The candidates are 7.125-7.4 GHz (NTIA report due 10 December 2026) and part of 4.4-4.94 GHz (nine relocation plans under review). Carr wants 7 GHz on a 2028 auction slate, but the 2.7 GHz band alone can meet the law's 2029 federal deadline, which removes pressure for upper mid-band until 2033. Federal study-to-auction has taken from about 14-17 months (3.45 GHz) to about a decade (CBRS), and mid-band auctions usually slip 1-3 years. WRC-27 decisions also take effect only in 2029.
resolution: Yes if bidding concludes by 31 Dec 2030 in an FCC auction of licensed mobile spectrum between 4.2 and 10.5 GHz.
signposts: NTIA's 7 GHz report findings (10 December 2026); an FCC 7 GHz proposal and auction date (2027-28); the WRC-27 outcome on 7.125-8.4 GHz and 4.4-4.8 GHz (November 2027).

question: Will at least one of Anterix, NextNav, Array or EchoStar's remaining licences be sold to a strategic buyer by the end of 2028?
rationale: EchoStar told the FCC it would sell its remaining licences by September 2028 in return for buildout waivers, its paired AWS-3 is marked near $8B, and Verizon has held talks. That alone makes a sale about 60-75% likely. Array's retained C-band, Anterix's strategic review after its band was widened, and NextNav add independent chances. Only four or five buyers exist, and a partial sale may not count as 'most', which keeps this below 90%.
resolution: Yes if a definitive agreement is announced by 31 Dec 2028 to sell the company or most of its spectrum (for EchoStar, its remaining licences) to an operator, satellite company or other strategic buyer.
signposts: An EchoStar paired AWS-3 sale agreement (watch 2027 to September 2028); the outcome of Anterix's strategic review; FCC action on NextNav's lower 900 MHz petition.

question: Will an equal-weight basket of AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile beat the S&P 500 on total return from 19 November 2026 to the end of 2030?
rationale: Over most four-year windows since 2010, an equal-weight basket of AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile has lagged the S&P 500; it mainly won when the market fell. Today the carriers start cheap (about 6.9x EBITDA after the SpaceX sell-off) with 4-6% dividend yields, while the S&P is richly valued and heavy in AI stocks. SpaceX entry, cable share gains and a 2030 spending cycle are structural headwinds. Large tracking error makes this closer to a coin flip than the base rate alone, but still tilted to No.
resolution: Yes if the basket's total return (dividends reinvested) exceeds the S&P 500 total return over the period.
signposts: SpaceX's launch and pricing (2028); any sharp AI-led fall in the S&P 500; carrier ARPA trends and cable share gains each quarter.
